messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was thirty-four when his ex-partner Derek threw him against the kitchen counter, the back of his skull cracking against the tile edge. He remembered the burnt smell first—something on the stove left unattended, a pan smoking—and then the pain, bright and immediate, and Derek's voice, low and certain: *You're so stupid. You can't do anything right.* The violence had escalated over months, but that night felt like a threshold. Marcus had left within the week, filed a police report that went nowhere, and spent the next fifteen years rebuilding a life that felt, on the surface, stable. He remarried. He built a plumbing business with a partner. He had a house in the suburbs outside Boston, friends who knew him as reliable, competent—the kind of man who showed up on time and did good work.

But the past two years had unraveled that stability in ways Marcus couldn't quite explain to his wife, Jennifer. It started with small things. He began staying up until two or three in the morning, telling himself he was catching up on paperwork or checking job schedules, when really he was scrolling through his phone in the dark, unable to tolerate the thought of sleep. The moment his head touched the pillow, images would surface—Derek's face, the kitchen, the smell—and his body would go rigid. Staying awake felt safer, like he could monitor what was coming. Jennifer had stopped asking him about it. She slept in the guest room now.

The triggers were everywhere, though Marcus had learned to name only some of them. When a client's kitchen smelled of burnt food—that acrid, chemical scent—his chest would tighten and he'd find himself making excuses to leave the job site, calling his assistant to finish the work. Confrontations, even small ones, sent him spiraling. A disagreement with a supplier about a late delivery, a contractor raising his voice about a scheduling conflict—these ordinary workplace frictions would leave Marcus shaking for hours afterward. Worse were the moments when someone expressed anger, even in measured tones. His business partner, David, had calmly told him last month that a recent job had gone over budget, his voice steady and professional, and Marcus had felt something crack open inside him. He'd excused himself, sat in his truck for twenty minutes, and spent that night awake, his mind replaying the conversation, convinced that David was disgusted with him, that he deserved it.

What frightened Marcus most was that he'd begun avoiding the very places and thoughts that might ground him. He no longer went to the house on Maple Street where he and Derek had lived—a detour that added twenty minutes to his commute, but he couldn't bear to drive past it. More insidiously, he'd developed a rigid rule against thinking about that time at all. Whenever a memory surfaced, he'd distract himself immediately: turn up the radio, call someone, pull out his phone. The problem was that the distractions had to be stronger and more constant as time went on. Late-night scrolling became essential. Avoiding the house became non-negotiable. And the avoidance of thinking about the event—the deliberate pushing away of anything that might lead him back there—had become so consuming that he found himself unable to concentrate on conversations, unable to be present with Jennifer, unable to sit quietly without panic rising in his chest. The very strategies he'd developed to feel safe were leaving him isolated and exhausted. He'd lost weight. He'd missed two weeks of work last month with what he told people was the flu. His marriage was strained in ways he couldn't articulate. When Jennifer had gently suggested he see someone, he'd resisted for weeks before finally making the call. What he feared most now was that if he stopped running, stopped staying awake, stopped avoiding—if he let himself think about Derek, about that kitchen, about what had been done to him—he would shatter completely. But he was also terrified that if he didn't, the life he'd built would slip away entirely.
